text: Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an exam is to stay up late at night. A study of two thousand university students suggests the opposite. Those who went to bed before midnight and slept for at least seven hours did better in their exams than those who stayed up. The researchers say the reason is simple: while we sleep, the brain sorts out what we learned during the day and moves it into long-term memory, so a student who sleeps well remembers more of what he or she has read. The team also found that short naps of about twenty minutes helped students who studied in the afternoon. They suggest that students should plan their sleep as carefully as their revision. 'If you have to choose between one more hour of reading and one more hour of sleep,' one researcher said, 'the sleep is usually the better investment.'

The city library has started a service called Books on the Move. From this month, readers can order books online and collect them from one of twelve lockers placed around the city, including three at underground stations. Each locker opens with a code sent to your phone, and you have three days to collect your book. If you do not collect it in time, the book goes back to the library and you pay a small fee of one dollar.
The service itself is free for the first year, and the library says it is aimed at people who work long hours and cannot reach a branch before it closes at five. In the first two weeks, more than three hundred people used the lockers, and most of them ordered novels. The library plans to add six more lockers near schools next spring if the trial is successful.

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for coming to the meeting at such short notice. Before I go through the figures, I want to talk about the change to our working hours. From June, everyone in this office will start at nine thirty instead of nine, and finish at six. We tested the idea in the design team for three months, and the results were better than we expected: they were late far less often, and the number of sick days fell by half. Nobody asked to go back to the old hours.
I know some of you are worried about the traffic in the morning. That is exactly why we chose nine thirty — the worst of the rush hour is over by then. If you have to collect a child from school at five, speak to your team leader, and we will find a way to make it work. Next week I will send round the full figures and a short form where you can tell us what you think.

A fire broke out in a clothing factory on the edge of the city late last night. Nobody was injured, and firefighters brought the fire under control within two hours. The manager of the factory said the fire had started in a store room, and that the damage is expected to cost about two hundred thousand dollars. An investigation into the cause will begin this morning.

A city in the north has decided to give free bus travel to all school students from September. The plan will cost about four million dollars a year and is expected to help around sixty thousand students. City officials say the aim is to reduce the number of cars outside schools in the morning. Some parents, however, say the buses are already full at that time, and that more buses will be needed before the plan can work.

A new report says that people who walk to work are happier with their daily journey than those who drive. Researchers asked five thousand workers in eight cities about their journeys. Those who walked gave the highest marks, followed by cyclists, while bus and underground passengers were the least satisfied, mainly because of crowding and delays. The report suggests that companies could help by paying for bicycles or by allowing staff to start work at different times.
